title: Dementia care is hard not because of the patient, but because of the caregiver who gets ground down
dek: The hard part of dementia care isn't the illness itself but the caregiver worn down day after day — care turns a wife into a nurse, forces a millennial to quit a job; love is the starting point but not the support, and the system hasn't caught these families yet.
why: This isn't a senior-health explainer but a sociologist's field honesty after walking into dementia households: no standard answers, only a reality you must see in advance.
who: Urban only-children born in the 80s and 90s, and anyone whose parents are starting to age while they've made no eldercare arrangements; also for those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care gap ends up pressing back onto every family
points.body: China's population over 60 is 323 million, 23% of the total; 35 million are disabled elders, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap hasn't been absorbed by the market or institutions, and the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient count is nearly 30% of the world's, and the host estimates that on average one in every 20 Chinese families is affected — for the first generation of only children, this may be a reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms, and the movies can't be trusted
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, the misunderstanding Tang Yong most wants to correct is that dementia patients have no uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from films, neighbors, or hearsay; the professor's incontinence in Still Alice is only one form. He has met a tailor who, after dementia, still noticed stains on a visitor's clothes and taught people to remove them with orange peel; and a man disabled by a car accident who, when he could only hum Liuyang River, wore an expression of intense focus. Dementia itself covers Alzheimer's, vascular dementia and other causes, and each person's life imprint lingers in a different way — care cannot be performed from a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal is paid for by national care insurance
points.body: Most people take the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: elders here stroll the supermarket and visit the café like residents, while staff play shopkeepers to keep the atmosphere normal. But the details the host adds expose how hard it is to replicate — the 23 homes built in 2009 cost more than 18 million euros, of which 17.8 million was borne by the government, and residents' fees are covered by long-term care-related systems. What Tang Yong saw in a low-income American nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to keep dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease, and the difference lies not in philosophy but in the state's payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough, and sacrifice will grind down the caregiver
points.body: The host sums up the caregiver's predicament precisely: many people swing back and forth between ‘I love my mom and dad so much’ and ‘I'm about to be crushed by my mom and dad’. Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse has to learn to bathe, feed, and handle emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by the relationship of nurse and patient. Long-term sacrifice is not a devotion to be romanticized: a daughter he interviewed in Guangzhou twenty years ago divorced and fell into severe depression after caring for her disabled father; the book also includes a millennial caregiver forced to quit a job under caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, the caregiver becomes a patient too.

points.h: The more you see, the less ground eldercare has
points.body: After years of researching eldercare, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his parents' old age. He is a first-generation only child, his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees the less ground he has; his research assistant even said after every interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how she would arrange things for her parents. Families with multiple children have friction too: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving gives an elder bedsores; only-child families lack manpower to share the load, and some who bring their parents to Shenzhen find rent, medical bills, and nanny fees stacking up faster than pensions rise. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing something every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that the caregiver must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elder who could at first paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others and not put brush to paper; another elder's husband reported new losses every week: his wife could not recognize the grandchild his daughter had just borne, and did not know where this child had come from. This day-after-day, irreversible downward slide drains a caregiver more than physical disability. The length of care is not the repetition of hardship but facing a small goodbye every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived, but it can't catch every elder
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 has spread to about 90 cities, with the official pace being universal coverage within the next two or three years. But Tang Yong cautions that long-term care insurance does not hand money to every elder; through unified assessment it mainly covers the moderately and severely disabled, paying for home care, meal delivery and other services; the mildly impaired may not qualify. The hardest part is mindset: sending parents to a nursing home in China is often equated with being unfilial, and elders, like the grandfather in the interviews, feel that after a month there their hair is nearly falling out. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the share who actively choose institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap will not disappear on its own.

terms.def: A closed community designed for severely dementia-impaired elders, where staff play residents to maintain a normal living atmosphere.
By Arthur Kleinman, arguing that care is not one-way help but a relationship.
Unpaid care borne by spouses, children and other family members, as distinct from hired nannies and care workers.
Social insurance that pays for the care services of disabled and dementia-impaired elders, not a cash subsidy.

quotes.text: I love my mom and dad so much, and I'm about to be crushed by my mom and dad — I swing back and forth between these two feelings.
So I think this care is probably still a relationship. In this relationship, the identities, emotions, and even the pace of life of both the caregiver and the cared-for change enormously.
It's like going down a slide — you're on the way down. So at that moment I thought, this kind of care really is long.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it probably isn't the whole condition of care. It still needs some external resources, including some social support, and so on.

Although the more I see, the more cases I come into contact with, it doesn't actually mean I have a very complete or very perfect plan for my parents' old age. Precisely because I've seen so many different stories, it has actually left me with more confusion.
